title: Drug classes II: pain, mood and antibiotics
note: NSAIDs block the cyclooxygenase enzymes that make prostaglandins; opioids activate opioid receptors; SSRIs block serotonin reuptake. Antibiotics are grouped by their bacterial target: the cell wall, the 70S ribosome, DNA replication, RNA synthesis or folate synthesis.

read.title: Selective toxicity
text: A good antimicrobial drug harms the microbe while sparing the patient, a property called selective toxicity. It is easiest to achieve when the drug's target exists only in the microbe. Bacteria offer several such targets because they differ so much from human cells.

The peptidoglycan cell wall is the clearest example: human cells have no wall, so beta-lactams and vancomycin, which block wall construction, are generally well tolerated. Bacterial 70S ribosomes differ from the 80S ribosomes in human cytoplasm, so aminoglycosides, tetracyclines and macrolides can block bacterial protein synthesis selectively. Bacteria must make their own folate, while humans absorb it from food, so sulfonamides spare human cells; trimethoprim binds the bacterial form of its target enzyme far more tightly than the human form.

Fungi and viruses are harder. Fungi are eukaryotes, so they share most of our machinery; antifungals usually target ergosterol, the sterol fungi use where human cells use cholesterol. Viruses use the host cell's own machinery, so antivirals must hit steps unique to the virus, such as viral enzymes. Acyclovir, for example, becomes active only after a viral enzyme modifies it, so it concentrates its action in infected cells.

q.q: Why are sulfonamides relatively safe for human cells?
o: Humans get folate from food rather than making it

q.q: Antifungal drugs often target ergosterol because
o: Ergosterol is found in bacterial walls

q.q: Why are antivirals hard to design?
o: Viruses use the host cell's own machinery
